title: Hello fetch
summary: The smallest cf.fetch round trip: the function GETs /hello on its own Lambda Web Function origin and copies one JSON field into a request header.
lesson: Proves the wiring contract: behavior, function association, origin id and the secret origin header. If the call fails the request still goes through, with x-hello-error.
expect: 200 JSON echo with headersFromFunction.x-hello-message = "hello from the origin" and x-hello-status = "200".

outcomes.label: The origin answered the call; its message rides on the forwarded request
The call failed; the request went through anyway with x-hello-error

gist: Before letting you in, the doorman phones the shop and writes its greeting on your ticket.

O.name: Shop
O.access: OAC signs it (SigV4), plus a secret x-origin-verify header

story: You knock on the door.
The doorman phones the shop first.
The shop says hello.
The doorman writes the hello on your ticket.
You walk in with your ticket.
The shop shows you what was written.
diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant V as Viewer
  participant F as CloudFront Function (viewer-request)
  participant O as Web Function origin "hello-fetch" (IamAuth + OAC)
  V->>F: GET /patterns/hello-fetch/
  F->>O: cf.fetch GET /hello
  O-->>F: {"message":"hello from the origin"}
  F->>F: x-hello-message, x-hello-status
  F->>O: forward the viewer request
  O-->>V: 200 JSON echo of the x-hello-* headers it received (the function's, plus any other x-hello-* the viewer sent) and x-origin-verify present

title: Cognito token check at the edge
summary: A CloudFront Function validates the viewer's Cognito access token with one cf.fetch and forwards the request with x-user-sub, replacing an API Gateway Lambda authorizer.
lesson: An AWS service reached without SigV4, and the auth decision made before the origin ever sees the request.
expect: Sign in as the demo user: the page gets a real Cognito access token from GET /patterns/cognito-auth/token (the password stays server-side), then calls whoami with it; the echo origin returns the x-user-sub and x-user-name the function injected. A forged x-user-sub is deleted before the check, so the real sub comes back. Without a token: 401 {"error":"missing_token"}, no call. A made-up token gets 401 invalid_token; Cognito unreachable gets 503 auth_unavailable (fail closed).

requests.label: Sign in as the demo user

outcomes.label: No bearer token: answered 401 at the edge, no call made
Cognito rejected the token: 401 invalid_token
Cognito unreachable: 503, failing closed
Cognito accepted the token; the origin saw the identity the function injected

gist: The doorman checks your ID card with the ID office before you get in.

C.name: ID office
C.service: Amazon Cognito user pool API (extra HTTPS origin)
C.access: public AWS endpoint; the access token is the credential

O.name: Your app
O.access: OAC signs it (SigV4), plus a secret x-origin-verify header

story: You knock, maybe holding an ID card.
The doorman rubs out any name you wrote yourself.
No ID card? Not today (401).
The doorman asks the ID office: is this card real?
Yes, and here is who you are.
The doorman writes your real name on your ticket.
The app greets you by name.
A fake card: not today (401).
The ID office did not answer, so nobody gets in (503).
waf: One rule on this pattern's path: a per-IP rate limit on the demo token route (/patterns/cognito-auth/token), 10 requests a minute. whoami itself has no rule.
diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant V as Viewer
  participant F as CloudFront Function (viewer-request)
  participant C as Cognito user pool endpoint (extra origin "cognito-auth")
  participant O as Echo Lambda Web Function "cognito-auth-echo" (IamAuth + OAC)
  V->>F: GET /patterns/cognito-auth/whoami, Authorization: Bearer token
  F->>F: delete viewer-supplied x-user-* headers
  alt no bearer token
    F-->>V: 401 missing_token (no call)
  else token present
    F->>C: cf.fetch POST / (X-Amz-Target GetUser, AccessToken)
    alt Cognito 2xx
      C-->>F: UserAttributes (sub, ...)
      F->>O: forward with x-user-sub, x-user-name
      O-->>V: 200 echo of the injected identity
    else Cognito non-2xx
      F-->>V: 401 invalid_token
    else error or timeout
      F-->>V: 503 auth_unavailable, x-cognito-auth-error
    end
  end

title: Custom authorizer with identity headers
summary: The function POSTs the viewer context (ip, uri, method, authorization, user-agent) to an authorizer Lambda and copies the returned x-tenant / x-role headers onto the request, or answers 403 itself.
lesson: The API Gateway Lambda authorizer 'context' pattern at the edge: viewer-supplied identity headers are stripped, the origin only ever sees values the authorizer granted, and every failure is a deny.
expect: Bearer demo-admin: 200 echo with identity x-tenant acme, x-role admin. demo-viewer is acme viewer, demo-globex is globex admin. A forged x-tenant / x-role is stripped: you still see the identity the authorizer granted. Any other token or none: 403 {"error":"forbidden"}. An unreachable authorizer: 503 {"error":"authorizer_unavailable"} (fail closed).

outcomes.label: Allowed as tenant acme, role admin: the origin saw only the headers the authorizer granted
Allowed as tenant acme, role viewer: any forged x-tenant / x-role was stripped
Allowed as tenant globex, role admin: a different identity from a different token
Allowed: the origin saw only the headers the authorizer granted
Denied by the authorizer: 403 from the edge
Authorizer unavailable: 503, failing closed

gist: The doorman asks the manager what you may do, and writes only that on your badge.

A.name: Manager
A.access: OAC signs it (SigV4), plus a secret x-origin-verify header

story: You knock with a pass.
The doorman rubs out any badge you made yourself.
He asks the manager: may this pass come in?
Yes: company acme, role admin.
You go in wearing exactly that badge.
The app sees your badge.
No.
The doorman says no (403); the app never hears of you.
The manager did not answer, so nobody gets in (503).
diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant V as Viewer
  participant F as CloudFront Function (viewer-request)
  participant A as Lambda Web Function "authorizer-headers" (IamAuth + OAC)
  V->>F: GET /patterns/authorizer-headers/echo, Authorization: Bearer demo-admin
  F->>F: delete viewer-supplied x-tenant, x-role
  F->>A: cf.fetch POST /authorize {ip, uri, method, headers}
  alt allow true
    A-->>F: {"allow":true,"headers":{"x-tenant":"acme","x-role":"admin"}}
    F->>A: forward with x-tenant, x-role (echo route)
    A-->>V: 200 echo of the identity headers
  else allow false
    A-->>F: {"allow":false,"headers":{}}
    F-->>V: 403 forbidden
  else non-2xx, bad JSON, error or timeout
    F-->>V: 503 authorizer_unavailable, x-authorizer-headers-error
  end

title: Bot check that fails open
summary: The function asks a mock bot-detection vendor and reads a block|tag|off policy from KVS at the same time; if the vendor is slower than the runtime's 1 s timeout or down, the request goes through anyway.
lesson: Third-party checks at the edge need a fail-open default: the runtime's fixed 1 s TimeoutError is the only latency limit (Date.now() does not advance across the await, so a self-timed budget never fires), and fetch + KVS is the one combination you may run in parallel.
expect: 200 JSON echo with x-bot-check: ok, x-bot-verdict human or bot with a score, and x-bot-policy from KVS (default tag). Add header x-mock-delay-ms: 1500 to see x-bot-check: unavailable with a TimeoutError after about 1 s: the request is forwarded anyway (fail open).

outcomes.label: Bot under a block policy: 403 block page
Vendor late or failing: forwarded anyway (fail open)
Vendor answered in time; verdict forwarded to the origin

gist: The doorman asks a robot spotter about you, but never waits more than a second: if it is slow, you get in anyway.

K.name: Notebook
K.access: associated with the function; read with cf.kvs()

B.name: Robot spotter
B.access: OAC signs it (SigV4), plus a secret x-origin-verify header

story: You knock.
The doorman rubs out any 'I am human' sticker you brought.
He asks the robot spotter about you, and waits one second at most.
Human or robot, with a score.
At the same time he reads the house rule in his notebook.
The rule: block robots, tag them, or ignore them.
A robot, and the rule says block: no entry (403).
Everyone else goes in, with the verdict on their ticket.
The app sees the verdict.
Spotter too slow (over a second) or broken? You go in anyway, marked unchecked.
diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant V as Viewer
  participant F as CloudFront Function (viewer-request)
  participant K as KVS
  participant B as Mock vendor Web Function "bot-check-fail-open" (IamAuth + OAC)
  V->>F: GET /patterns/bot-check-fail-open/echo
  F->>F: delete viewer-supplied x-bot-* headers
  par Promise.allSettled
    F->>B: cf.fetch POST /check {path, ip, user-agent, accept-language}
    B-->>F: {"verdict":"human" or "bot","score":N}
  and
    F->>K: get("bot-policy")
    K-->>F: block, tag or off (default tag)
  end
  alt bot and policy block
    F-->>V: 403 block page
  else anything else
    F->>B: forward with x-bot-check, x-bot-verdict, x-bot-score, x-bot-policy
    B-->>V: 200 echo of the x-bot-* headers
  end
  Note over F: TimeoutError (over 1 s), error or non-200 means x-bot-check: unavailable, forward

title: Sticky A/B variant, KVS warm set over a DynamoDB global table
summary: The function reads the user's variant from KVS and only calls the origin on a miss; the origin assigns it once in DynamoDB and fills KVS lazily.
lesson: Fetch only on a miss: pay the extra execution once per key, then serve from the edge until TTL evicts it.
expect: JSON echo with x-ab-variant and x-ab-source; the response carries x-ab-hooks: request+response and Set-Cookie uid=<16 hex> (first visit), set by the viewer-response function, not the origin. x-ab-variant is A or B, x-ab-source origin on a first visit (one call) and kvs on a return visit (no call), plus Set-Cookie ab=<variant>. Any failure falls back to x-ab-variant control, x-ab-source fallback and x-ab-error, with no ab cookie.

outcomes.label: KVS hit: variant served from the edge, no call
KVS miss: one call assigned the variant
Lookup failed: control variant, no ab cookie

gist: The doorman looks up which room you got last time; only new guests get a room picked, once.

K.name: Notebook
K.access: read by the function; written by the loader and evictor (UpdateKeys)

L.name: Host
L.access: OAC signs it (SigV4), plus a secret x-origin-verify header

D.name: Big ledger
D.access: the loader's IAM role; its stream feeds an evictor Lambda

story: You arrive, maybe with your wristband.
No wristband? The doorman makes you a new one.
He looks you up in his notebook.
Found: same room as last time, no phone call.
Not found: he asks the host to pick a room.
The host writes your room in the big ledger, once.
And copies it into the doorman's notebook for next time.
Room A or room B.
Something broke: you get the normal room.
You walk to your room.
The room answers.
On the way out, the greeter puts your wristbands on.
You get your page.
When the ledger changes, the notebook changes too.
diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant V as Viewer
  participant F as viewer-request function
  participant K as KVS
  participant L as Loader Web Function (IamAuth + OAC)
  participant D as DynamoDB global table
  participant R as viewer-response function
  V->>F: GET /patterns/ab-global-table/ (cookie uid, or none)
  F->>F: drop viewer x-ab-set-*, mint a uid if missing
  F->>K: get(uid)
  alt KVS hit
    K-->>F: A or B (x-ab-source: kvs, no call)
  else miss
    F->>L: cf.fetch POST /assign/uid
    L->>D: conditional PutItem (or read the existing item)
    L->>K: UpdateKeys put uid
    L-->>F: {"variant":"A" or "B"} (x-ab-source: origin)
  else any failure
    F->>F: x-ab-variant: control, x-ab-source: fallback, x-ab-error
  end
  F->>L: forward with x-ab-variant, x-ab-set-uid, x-ab-set-variant
  L-->>R: 200 JSON echo
  R->>R: Set-Cookie uid (new uid), Set-Cookie ab (A or B only), x-ab-hooks
  R-->>V: response
  Note over D,K: TTL expiry or an edit streams to the evictor Lambda, which deletes or rewrites the KVS key

title: Edge signal to SQS, no Lambda
summary: The request function fires one small JSON event with cf.beacon into an SQS FIFO queue through an API Gateway service integration; the response function beacons a second 'served' event only on demand (x-signal-sample: 1). Its 5xx condition never fires: CloudFront does not run viewer-response when the origin answers 400 or more.
lesson: API Gateway is the signing proxy for SigV4-only services; cf.beacon makes the signal fire-and-forget (still the one call per invocation, available wherever cf.fetch is); and a response-side call runs on cache hits too, so it must be rare by construction.
expect: JSON echo with headersFromFunction.x-signal = "beacon" and x-signal-served: skipped on the response; one requested event in the queue. Send x-signal-sample: 1 for x-signal-served: beacon and a second queue message. /boom returns 503 with NO x-signal-served header: CloudFront skips viewer-response on origin 4xx/5xx.

outcomes.label: One beacon: the response function skipped its call
Two beacons: requested and served

gist: The doorman drops a note in the mailbox as you pass, without slowing you down.

A.name: Mail clerk
A.service: API Gateway REST API with an SQS integration

Q.name: Mailbox
Q.access: API Gateway's IAM role sends the message

The doorman drops a 'someone came' note in the mail slot.
The clerk puts it in the mailbox.

You reach the room.

title: Private routing decision from a VPC origin
summary: The function asks an internal ALB (CloudFront VPC origin, no public address) which backend a tenant belongs to, then rewrites the URI to that backend.
lesson: Call a private service from the edge without exposing it, and keep a KVS kill switch that skips the network call entirely.
expect: JSON with backend "blue" or "green" (stable per tenant) and headersFromFunction.x-backend set by the function. A failed call forwards unchanged: backend "none" and x-vpc-private-routing-error.

outcomes.label: Kill switch off: no call, request forwarded unchanged
The private ALB chose a backend; the URI was rewritten
Routing call failed: forwarded unchanged

gist: The doorman asks a back office nobody else can reach which room is yours.

K.name: Notebook
K.access: associated with the function; read with cf.kvs()

A.name: Back office
A.service: Internal Application Load Balancer, Lambda target
A.access: CloudFront VPC origin: private subnets, no public address

story: You arrive and say which company you are with.
The doorman checks the on/off switch in his notebook.
Switch off: no question asked, you go in as you are.
Switch on: he asks the back office where your company sits.
Blue room or green room.

sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant V as Viewer
  participant F as CloudFront Function (viewer-request)
  participant K as KVS
  participant A as VPC origin, internal ALB, Lambda target
  V->>F: GET /patterns/vpc-private-routing/whoami?tenant=acme
  F->>K: get("routing-kill-switch")
  alt kill switch "off"
    F->>F: x-backend: off (no call)

    F->>A: cf.fetch GET /route?tenant=acme

  end

  A-->>V: 200 JSON from the chosen backend, or backend "none"

title: Read-through config: KVS first, fetch on a miss, hot keys promoted
summary: The function reads a key's config (a tenant's plan, a model route, a rate limit) from KVS; on a miss it makes one call to the origin, which counts the read, and a key read 5 times in a minute is promoted into KVS for 10 minutes.
lesson: Read through KVS: a hit costs no call, a miss costs one, and only hot keys earn a place in KVS, written off the request path. Fail open: serve the expired copy, else a default, and always forward the request.
expect: 200 JSON echo with x-config-source origin and x-config-hits n/5 on a cold key; after 5 reads in a minute, about a minute later x-config-source kvs with no call.

outcomes.label: Fresh copy in KVS: answered at the edge, no call
Miss: fetched from the origin, and that read made the key hot, so it gets promoted to KVS
Miss: one call fetched it from the origin and counted the read
The call failed: served the expired copy from KVS
The call failed and KVS had nothing: default config

gist: The doorman looks in his notebook first and phones the clerk only when it is not there; settings asked for often get copied into the notebook by themselves.

K.name: Notebook
K.access: read by the function; written by the promoter (UpdateKeys)

D.name: Tally board
D.access: the origin Lambda's IAM role; its stream feeds the promoter

story: You ask for the settings for acme.
The doorman rubs out any settings you wrote yourself.
He looks in his notebook first.
A fresh copy is there: no phone call.
Not there, or too old: he asks the config clerk.
The clerk adds a tick to acme's tally for this minute.
Here are the settings, and the tally so far.
The clerk did not answer: an old copy, or the default.
You go in carrying the settings.
You see which settings you got, and where from.
Behind the scenes, separate from your visit:
Five ticks in one minute: acme is popular.
The promoter pins a ten-minute marker on the board.
The marker is up.
The promoter copies acme's settings into the notebook.
Ten minutes later the marker falls off.
The promoter rubs acme out of the notebook again.
diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant V as Viewer
  participant F as CloudFront Function (viewer-request)
  participant K as KVS
  participant L as Config Web Function "kvs-config-plus-fetch" (IamAuth + OAC)
  participant D as DynamoDB hot-key table
  participant P as Promoter Lambda
  V->>F: GET /patterns/kvs-config-plus-fetch/acme
  F->>F: drop viewer x-config-*
  F->>K: get("cfg-acme")
  alt fresh entry
    K-->>F: {"exp":...,"config":{...}} (x-config-source: kvs, no call)
  else miss or expired
    F->>L: cf.fetch GET /config/acme
    L->>D: ADD hits on hits#35;acme#35;<minute>
    L-->>F: {"config":{...},"hits":3,"threshold":5} (x-config-source: origin)
  else call fails
    F->>F: expired entry (kvs-stale), else DEFAULT_CONFIG (default), x-config-error
  end
  F->>L: forward with x-config, x-config-key, x-config-source
  L-->>V: 200 JSON echo of the x-config-* headers
  Note over D,P: off the request path, from the table's stream
  D-->>P: counter reached 5
  P->>D: put marker kvs#35;acme (TTL = now + 10 min)
  D-->>P: marker written
  P->>K: UpdateKeys put cfg-acme (reaches the edge in about a minute)
  D-->>P: marker removed by TTL
  P->>K: UpdateKeys delete cfg-acme

title: POST failover: origin health probe + secondary
summary: Failover for POST traffic, which origin groups cannot do: when gated on, the request function probes GET /health on the primary with cf.fetch and, if it times out (the runtime's fixed 1 s) or is down, sends the POST to a secondary Lambda Web Function with selectRequestOriginById. GET/HEAD also get a runtime origin group (S3 mirror on 5xx).
lesson: Origin groups only fail over GET/HEAD/OPTIONS, and viewer-response never runs for status 400+, so for POST the edge function is the only place to decide before the request is sent. Gate the probe (KVS health-probe) or you pay a call per request; fail open when the call is unavailable.
expect: The primary's /health sleeps 1.5 s, past the fixed 1 s runtime timeout: x-health-probe: unhealthy:timeout, x-route: fallback, and the secondary answers the POST: x-served-by: secondary, x-fallback: true, body servedBy "secondary".

outcomes.label: Primary timed out or down: the POST went to the secondary
Probe healthy: the POST went to the primary
Probe gated off: straight to the primary, no call

gist: Before passing on your order, the doorman checks the main kitchen is quick; if not, the backup kitchen cooks it.

K.name: Notebook
K.access: associated with the function; read with cf.kvs()

P.name: Main kitchen
P.access: OAC signs it (SigV4), plus a secret x-origin-verify header

S.name: Backup kitchen
S.access: OAC signs it (SigV4), plus a secret x-origin-verify header

The doorman checks whether to test the kitchen first.
No test: the order goes to the main kitchen.
Test: are you quick today? He waits one second at most.
The kitchen answers.
Quick: your order goes to the main kitchen.

sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant V as Viewer
  participant F as viewer-request function
  participant K as KVS
  participant P as Primary Web Function "origin-health-fallback" (IamAuth + OAC)
  participant S as Secondary Web Function "origin-health-fallback-secondary" (POST standby)
  participant M as S3 static mirror (GET and HEAD)
  participant R as viewer-response function
  V->>F: POST /patterns/origin-health-fallback/infer?probe=on
  F->>K: get("health-probe") (?probe= overrides)
  alt probe gate off, or the call unavailable
    F->>F: x-health-probe: off or unavailable, x-route: primary (fail open)

  R-->>V: response (viewer-response does not run on 4xx or 5xx)

title: Per-resource authorization for AI agents
summary: An agent sends a scoped token on every request; the function POSTs { action, resource, token } to an authorization service and forwards the request only when it answers allowed: true.
lesson: A token says who the agent is, not whether it may act on this resource right now. Ask on every request at the edge: denied calls never reach the backend, and allowed reads can still be cache hits because viewer request runs before the cache.
expect: No Authorization header: 401 {"error":"unauthorized"}, no call made. Authorization: Bearer demo-agent-token on /orders/48291: 200 order JSON (cacheable); on /orders/70113 or with any write method: 403 {"error":"forbidden"}. An unreachable authorization service: 503 {"error":"authz_unavailable"} (fail closed).

outcomes.label: No token: answered 401 at the edge, no call made
Allowed: the order came back (and may be cached)
Not allowed for this resource: 403 from the edge
Authorization service unreachable: 503, failing closed

gist: A robot helper wants an order; the doorman asks the permission desk every single time.

A.name: Permission desk
A.access: OAC signs it (SigV4), plus a secret x-origin-verify header

story: A robot helper asks for an order, holding a pass.
No pass? Not today (401).
The doorman asks the desk: may this robot see this order?
Yes.
The robot goes to the pickup shelf.
It gets the order, maybe already waiting on the shelf.
No.
Not yours (403); the shop never hears of it.
The desk did not answer, so no (503).
diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant V as Agent
  participant F as CloudFront Function (viewer-request)
  participant C as CloudFront cache
  participant A as Lambda Web Function "agent-authz" (IamAuth + OAC)
  V->>F: GET /patterns/agent-authz/orders/48291, Authorization: Bearer demo-agent-token
  alt no Authorization header, or an empty one
    F-->>V: 401 unauthorized (no call made)
  end
  F->>A: cf.fetch POST /v1/check {action: "read", resource: uri, token}
  alt allowed true
    A-->>F: {"allowed":true}
    F->>C: forward the request
    C-->>V: 200 order (cache hit, or from the orders route, cached 60 s)
  else allowed false
    A-->>F: {"allowed":false}
    F-->>V: 403 forbidden
  else non-2xx, bad JSON, error or timeout
    F-->>V: 503 authz_unavailable, x-agent-authz-error
  end

title: Markdown on demand for AI agents
summary: An AI agent (Accept: text/markdown, or an AI bot labelled by AWS WAF Bot Control) gets a markdown copy of the page when KVS says one exists; otherwise the HTML, and the function fires one cf.beacon with the page URI into SQS FIFO so a worker converts it offline.
lesson: The one network call is the beacon, so 'does markdown exist yet?' must come from KVS, which the worker writes after it stores the .md. A beacon is best effort and billed: a dropped one only means the next agent request asks again, and the FIFO queue deduplicates the burst.
expect: A browser: 200 text/html, x-markdown: skipped. With Accept: text/markdown the first time: 200 text/html and x-markdown: queued (one beacon). Wait about a minute (worker + KVS propagation), then the same request: 200 text/markdown, x-markdown: served. Reset this page: 200 JSON, x-markdown: reset; about a minute later the agent request is queued again.

requests.label: A browser asks for the page

outcomes.label: A markdown copy exists: the agent got the .md
No markdown yet: the agent got the HTML, and one beacon asked for a copy
A browser: the normal HTML page, no KVS read and no beacon
Reset queued: the worker deletes the page's KVS key and keeps the .md for edges that still have it. In about a minute the next agent request is queued again

gist: People get the normal page; robots that prefer markdown get a markdown copy when one exists, and if not, the doorman orders one for next time.
waf: Bot Control in count mode labels AI bots; two count rules write x-amzn-waf-ai-agent on every request here: the bot's name, or none.

K.name: Notebook
K.access: read by the function; written by the worker

A.name: Mail clerk
A.service: API Gateway REST API with an SQS integration

Q.name: Mailbox
Q.access: API Gateway's IAM role sends the message

W.name: Rewriter
W.access: triggered by the queue; writes the .md and the KVS key, a reset deletes the key

story: Every visitor passes the gatekeeper, who knows AI robots by sight (AWS WAF Bot Control).
He pins a badge on each one for the doorman: the robot's name, or none.
A visitor asks the doorman to forget a page's markdown copy.
He drops a 'please forget' note in the mail slot.
The clerk puts the note in the mailbox.
The doorman answers himself: the note is on its way.
The rewriter picks up the note.
It crosses the copy out of the notebook, gone in about a minute; the copy stays on the shelf.
A person asks for a page.
A person gets the normal page, no notebook, no note.
A robot that prefers markdown asks for the page.
The doorman checks his notebook for a markdown copy.
Yes, and here is where it is.
He sends the robot to the markdown copy.
No copy yet: he drops a 'please convert' note in the mail slot.
The clerk puts the note in the mailbox.
Meanwhile the robot gets the normal page.
The rewriter picks up the note.
It reads the page and writes a markdown copy.
It notes the copy in the notebook, ready in about a minute.
The shelf hands over the page.
On the way out, the greeter says which one you got.
diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant V as Viewer (browser or agent)
  participant B as AWS WAF (Bot Control, count)
  participant F as viewer-request function
  participant K as KVS
  participant S as S3 bucket (pages + .md)
  participant A as API Gateway REST API (x-api-key)
  participant Q as SQS FIFO queue
  participant W as worker Lambda (turndown)
  participant R as viewer-response function
  V->>B: GET /patterns/markdown-on-demand/...
  B->>F: request + x-amzn-waf-ai-agent: the bot's name (gptbot, claudebot, ...) or none
  alt reset a page (anyone, a page under this path)
    V->>F: GET /patterns/markdown-on-demand/reset?page=guide.html
    F-)A: cf.beacon POST /patterns/convert {action: reset, uri, at}
    A-)Q: SendMessage (at: a reset is never a repeat)
    F-->>V: 200 JSON reset queued (x-markdown: reset, no-store)
    Q-)W: {action: reset, uri}
    W->>K: DeleteKey md:<uri> only, the .md stays (leaves the edge in about a minute)
  else a browser (no markdown in Accept, x-amzn-waf-ai-agent: none)
    V->>F: GET /patterns/markdown-on-demand/guide.html
    F->>S: GET guide.html (x-markdown: skipped, no KVS read, no beacon)
  else an agent (Accept: text/markdown, or a bot name in x-amzn-waf-ai-agent)
    V->>F: GET guide.html as an agent
    F->>K: get md:/patterns/markdown-on-demand/guide.html
    alt key found
      K-->>F: /patterns/markdown-on-demand/guide.md
      F->>S: GET guide.md (x-markdown: served)
    else KeyNotFound
      F-)A: cf.beacon POST /patterns/convert {uri, minute}
      A-)Q: SendMessage (dedup on the body)
      F->>S: GET guide.html (x-markdown: queued)
      Q-)W: {uri, minute}
      W->>S: GET guide.html, PUT guide.md (overwrites one left by a reset)
      W->>K: PutKey md:<uri> = guide.md (reaches the edge in about a minute)
    end
  end
  S-->>R: 200
  R-->>V: response + x-markdown, Vary: Accept, User-Agent

title: Edge waiting room
summary: A virtual waiting room at the edge. A new browser (past AWS WAF's CAPTCHA) spends the function's one cf.fetch to draw a ticket from a DynamoDB counter (API Gateway, no Lambda); every refresh after that compares the signed ticket cookie with a watermark in KVS, with no call. An admission Lambda raises the watermark once a minute.
lesson: The queue is two integers, a counter and a watermark, and membership is an HMAC-signed cookie: the one network call is spent once per viewer, never per refresh. Here the call IS the protection, so it fails closed, the reverse of 03 and 08.
expect: Try it (a fetch, not a page load): 503, x-wr: browsers-only, no ticket. Open it in a browser tab instead: one AWS WAF CAPTCHA (only on this path), then a waiting page with your ticket and your position; within about two minutes (one admission tick plus KVS propagation) a 302 sets wr_a and the protected origin's JSON says x-wr: admitted.

skipUnlessSeen.note: No CAPTCHA this time: your browser already had AWS WAF's token.
No new ticket: you already hold one, so the doorman makes no call.
No wait: your number was already being served.

states.label: AWS WAF asks for a CAPTCHA on the first visit: solve it in the frame below to join the queue
AWS WAF's silent challenge: your browser is proving it is a browser
Ticket {1} drawn: the function's one cf.fetch added one to the counter
In line: position about {1}, roughly {2} min. Each refresh is a KVS read, no call
The queue is paused: you keep your place in line
The queue is starting: the page tries again in a moment
Busy: the counter could not be reached, so no ticket yet; the page retries

outcomes.label: What a bot gets: the viewer-request function answers 503 browsers-only, so no ticket is drawn
Admitted: the protected origin answered
Left the line: your place is freed for the next person, and your ticket, pass and WAF token are cleared. Open it in a tab to start over (CAPTCHA first)

waf: Bot Control in count mode gives each browser a token id; a first page load gets one CAPTCHA, and the silent challenge takes over once it expires, so scripts never draw a ticket.
gist: A gatekeeper stops scripts; the doorman hands real visitors a numbered ticket and lets them in when their number comes up.

K.name: Notebook
K.access: read by the function; the admission Lambda raises queue-state (UpdateKeys)

A.name: Ticket machine
A.service: API Gateway REST API with a DynamoDB integration (no Lambda)

D.name: Counter
D.access: API Gateway's IAM role runs UpdateItem ADD n 1

L.name: Usher
L.access: EventBridge schedule; reads the counters, writes KVS

story: A script asks for the shop: not a page load.
The gatekeeper sets no puzzle for that and lets it through.
The doorman checks his notebook, as for everyone.
No ticket for a script: come back in a browser. No phone call.
You ask to leave the line, with your ticket.
The gatekeeper lets it through: not a page load.
The doorman checks his notebook and your ticket's signature: still in line?
Yes: he drops a note to the ticket machine and doesn't wait for an answer.
The machine crosses your number off: even sent twice, it is crossed off once.
The doorman tears up your ticket and your pass, and the gatekeeper's too.
Your browser asks for the shop, without a pass from the gatekeeper.
The gatekeeper tests your browser: a CAPTCHA the first time, a silent check after that; then the page reloads.
Back again, now with the gatekeeper's pass.
The gatekeeper lets you through and tells the doorman your pass number.
The doorman checks his notebook: which number is being served?
You have no ticket yet: he asks the ticket machine for one.
The machine adds one to the counter.
Your number comes back.
You get the waiting room, and your ticket as a signed cookie.
Your browser comes back with your ticket, every few seconds.
The doorman checks your ticket and his notebook: no phone call.
Still waiting: here is your place in line.
Every minute, the usher looks at how many are waiting.
And moves the 'now serving' number up past five people still waiting, skipping anyone who left.
Your browser checks back; your number is being served.
The doorman gives you an entry pass, good for two minutes.
You come back with the entry pass.
The doorman lets you into the shop.
The shop answers.
diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant V as Browser
  participant W as AWS WAF (this path only)
  participant F as viewer-request function
  participant K as KVS
  participant A as API Gateway REST API (x-api-key)
  participant D as DynamoDB counters
  participant L as admission Lambda (every minute)
  alt a script (not a page load)
    V->>W: GET /patterns/edge-waiting-room/shop, Accept: */*
    W->>F: passes: CAPTCHA and challenge apply to page loads only
    F->>K: get queue-state, queue-secret-cur, queue-secret-prev
    F-->>V: 503 browsers-only + Retry-After: 5, no ticket, no call
  else leave the line
    V->>W: GET /patterns/edge-waiting-room/leave + wr_t
    W->>F: passes: not a page load
    F->>K: get queue-state, queue-secret-cur, queue-secret-prev
    F-)A: cf.beacon POST /patterns/leave {epoch, ticket}, only for a signed ticket still in line
    A-)D: UpdateItem e<epoch>-left ADD freed {ticket} (a number set)
    F-->>V: 200 left (x-wr-place: freed), wr_t, wr_a and aws-waf-token expired
  else a browser
    V->>W: GET /patterns/edge-waiting-room/shop, no aws-waf-token
    W-->>V: 405 CAPTCHA on the first visit (silent challenge once it expires)
    V->>W: GET + aws-waf-token
    W->>F: request + x-amzn-waf-wr-token-id (Bot Control label, interpolated)
  end
  F->>K: get queue-state, queue-secret-cur, queue-secret-prev
  F->>A: cf.fetch POST /patterns/enqueue {epoch, shard}
  A->>D: UpdateItem e<epoch>-<shard> ADD n 1
  D-->>F: {"n": 42}, ticket = (42 - 1) * 8 + shard
  F-->>V: 200 waiting page + wr_t (no-store)
  loop every 5 s
    V->>F: GET + wr_t
    F->>K: get queue-state
    F-->>V: 200 waiting page, position, no call
  end
  L->>D: BatchGetItem the 8 shards, GetItem the freed set
  L->>K: UpdateKeys queue-state {serving past STEP waiting tickets, freed ones skipped}
  V->>F: GET + wr_t, ticket < serving
  F-->>V: 302 same URL + wr_a (bound to this client, 120 s)
  V->>F: GET + wr_a
  F->>A: forward (x-wr: admitted)
  A-->>V: 200 from the protected origin
